To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combination of a novel antibiotic with a novel host-targeted drug can synergistically inhibit bacterial growth and virulence, and that the antibiotic is effective even in the presence of a multidrug resistance efflux pump.

(i) the host-pathogen interface is a promising therapeutic target to counter bacterial resistance to antibiotics, (ii) the exploitation of host and/or pathogen-directed therapies to target the host-pathogen interaction is a novel approach that can be used to combat bacterial resistance, (iii) host- and pathogen-directed therapies can be exploited as novel combined strategies to counteract bacterial resistance.

(i) the host-pathogen interplay is crucial for the establishment of a successful bacterial infection; (ii) the host immune response can be exploited to develop novel antimicrobial therapies; (iii) the host immune system and bacterial pathogens can be targeted simultaneously to achieve synergistic antimicrobial effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new therapeutic agents for the treatment of infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
the identification, validation, and application of novel host- and pathogen-directed therapies for the treatment of infections caused by multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria.
the development of novel antimicrobial strategies based on the exploitation of the host-pathogen interaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the development of novel antimicrobial agents, alone or in combination with host-directed strategies, represents the only viable option for the treatment of multidrug resistant bacterial infections.

the use of antibiotics should be restricted only to the cases of severe infections, while the use of antibiotics for prophylaxis or as a preventive treatment should be avoided, and that antibiotics should be used for the shortest possible period.

the current state of knowledge of the mechanisms of antibiotic action and resistance in bacteria is far more complex than previously thought, with many more mechanisms and players involved than the classical ones, which have been the subject of intense research for the last 50 years or more.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new approach for the discovery and development of novel antibacterial drugs, which is not only effective against multidrug-resistant bacteria but also safe for human use.

the combination of host- and pathogen-directed therapies could be a promising strategy for combating multidrug resistance in bacterial infections, but the efficacy and safety of this approach need to be evaluated in clinical studies before its clinical application.
we have shown that a combination therapy, based on a combination of the host-directed drug dapsone and a pathogen-directed drug, is able to overcome the resistance mechanisms of the pathogen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of host-directed therapy with a conventional antibiotic may be effective in combating bacterial resistance, and this strategy could also be extended to other pathogen species.
, by combining host-directed therapies with pathogen-directed antibiotics, we can achieve a synergistic reduction in the pathogen burden.
the use of novel combined host- and pathogen-directed therapies is an important and timely strategy for combatting bacterial multidrug resistance (MDR).
